claim: About 35% of mental illnesses begin prior to age 14
source: Indeed, about 35% of mental illnesses begin prior to age 14 (Solmi et al., 2022), motivating efforts to identify vulnerability markers of psychopathology early on Lynch et al., 2021.
evidence: Supported by citation to Solmi et al., 2022

claim: The ABCD study aimed for 50% of their sample to exhibit early signs of internalizing/externalizing symptoms
source: To ensure that the study had enough statistical power to characterize a large variety of developmental trajectories, the ABCD study aimed for 50% of their sample to exhibit early signs of internalizing/externalizing symptoms (Garavan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garavan et al., 2018

claim: Several neurodevelopmental conditions have been increasingly conceptualized as a continuum that encompasses subclinical expressions within the general population, intermediate outcomes, and a full diagnosis at the severe tail of the distribution
source: While not without controversy, several neurodevelopmental conditions have been increasingly conceptualized as a continuum that encompasses subclinical expressions within the general population, intermediate outcomes, and a full diagnosis at the severe tail of the distribution (Abu-Akel et al., 2019; Lundström et al., 2012; Robinson et al., 2016; Robinson et al., 2011).

claim: Psychopathology can be conceptualized along a hierarchical structure, with a general psychopathology (or p factor) at the apex, reflecting an individual's susceptibility to develop any common form of psychopathology
source: Psychopathology can be conceptualized along a hierarchical structure, with a general psychopathology (or p factor) at the apex, reflecting an individual's susceptibility to develop any common form of psychopathology (Caspi et al., 2014; Kotov et al., 2017; Lahey et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caspi et al., 2014; Kotov et al., 2017; Lahey et al., 2017

claim: Five dimensions of psychopathology (internalizing, externalizing, neurodevelopmental, detachment, and somatoform) were derived using exploratory factor analysis on parent-reported behavioral data from the ABCD dataset
source: Recently, five dimensions of psychopathology, that is, internalizing, externalizing, neurodevelopmental, detachment, and somatoform (Michelini et al., 2019), were derived using exploratory factor analysis on parent-reported behavioral data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) dataset, a large community-based cohort of typically developing children (Casey et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Michelini et al., 2019 and Casey et al., 2018

claim: Transmodal association systems, such as the default mode network, have a long maturation time, which renders them particularly vulnerable for development of psychopathology
source: Indeed, compared to sensory and motor regions, transmodal association systems, such as the default mode network, have a long maturation time, which renders them particularly vulnerable for development of psychopathology (Paquola et al., 2019; Park et al., 2022b; Sydnor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Paquola et al., 2019; Park et al., 2022b; Sydnor et al., 2021

claim: The main analyses included 5251 unrelated children (2577 female [49%], 9.94 ± 0.62 years old, 19 sites)
source: After excluding participants with incomplete structural MRI, resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), or behavioral data, MRI preprocessing, and quality control, and after excluding sites with less than 20 participants, our main analyses included 5251 unrelated children (2577 female [49%], 9.94 ± 0.62 years old, 19 sites).
evidence: Directly stated participant demographics from the study

claim: The sample was divided into Discovery (N = 3504, i.e., 2/3 of the dataset) and Replication (N = 1747, i.e., 1/3 of the dataset) subsamples
source: We divided this sample into Discovery (N = 3504, i.e., 2/3 of the dataset) and Replication (N = 1747, i.e., 1/3 of the dataset) subsamples, using randomized data partitioning with both subsamples being matched on age, sex, ethnicity, acquisition site, and overall psychopathology (i.e., scores of the first principal component derived from the 118 items of the Achenbach CBCL Achenbach and Rescorla, 2013).

claim: PLS analysis revealed five significant LCs (all p = 0.001 after permuting the first five LCs 10,000 times, accounting for site and false discovery rate [FDR]) in the discovery sample
source: PLS analysis revealed five significant LCs (all p = 0.001 after permuting the first five LCs 10,000 times, accounting for site and false discovery rate [FDR]) in the discovery sample.
evidence: Statistical results from PLS analysis with permutation testing

claim: The five significant latent components explained 21%, 4%, 3%, 3%, and 2% of covariance between the imaging and behavioral data, respectively
source: They explained 21%, 4%, 3%, 3%, and 2% of covariance between the imaging and behavioral data, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical results from PLS analysis shown in text and figure

claim: LC1 recapitulated a previously described p factor and strongly correlated (r = 0.64, p < 0.001) with the p factor derived from CBCL items by Michelini et al., 2019
source: LC1 (r = 0.36, permuted p < 0.001; out-of-sample generalizability of model statistics: r = 0.03, permuted p < 0.001; Figure 2a) recapitulated a previously described p factor (Alnæs et al., 2018; Caspi et al., 2014; Elliott et al., 2018; Kaczkurkin et al., 2018; Kebets et al., 2019; Lahey et al., 2011; Romer et al., 2018; Shanmugan et al., 2016; Van Dam et al., 2017), and strongly correlated (r = 0.64, p < 0.001; Supplementary file 1a) with the p factor derived from CBCL items by Michelini et al., 2019.
evidence: Statistical correlation with previously published factor and citations

claim: All symptom items loaded positively on LC1
source: All symptom items loaded positively on LC1 – which is expected given prior data showing that every prevalent mental disorder loads positively on the p factor (Lahey et al., 2012).
evidence: Observation from data analysis with citation to prior work

claim: The top behavioral loadings for LC1 included being inattentive/distracted, impulsive behavior, mood changes, rule breaking, and arguing
source: The top behavioral loadings included being inattentive/distracted, impulsive behavior, mood changes, rule breaking, and arguing (Figure 2b, see Supplementary file 1b for all behavior loadings).
evidence: Results shown in figure and text

claim: Greater psychopathology in LC1 was mainly associated with volume and thickness reductions, while the pattern of surface area associations was more mixed encompassing increases as well as decreases
source: Greater (i.e., worse) psychopathology was, overall, mainly associated with volume and thickness reductions, while the pattern of surface area associations was more mixed encompassing increases as well as decreases (Figure 2c, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for uncorrected structural imaging loadings, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for subcortical volume loadings).
evidence: Results from structural imaging analysis shown in figures

claim: Greater psychopathology in LC1 was associated with increased RSFC between the default and executive control, default, dorsal and ventral attention networks
source: Greater psychopathology was also associated with patterns of large-scale network organization (Schaefer et al., 2018; Yeo et al., 2011), namely increased RSFC between the default and executive control, default, dorsal and ventral attention networks, and decreased RSFC between the two attention networks, between visual and default networks, and between control and attention networks (Figure 2d, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for a zoom on subcortical–cortical loadings, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for uncorrected RSFC loadings).
evidence: Results from functional connectivity analysis shown in figures

claim: LC2 contrasted internalizing vs. externalizing symptoms
source: LC2 (r = 0.34, permuted p < 0.001; out-of-sample generalizability of model statistics: r = 0.05, permuted p < 0.001; Figure 3a) contrasted internalizing vs. externalizing symptoms – two broad dimensions that are driven by covariation of symptoms among internalizing and externalizing disorders (Lahey et al., 2012; Lahey et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of LC2 with citations to prior work

claim: Higher behavior loadings in LC2 indicated increased internalizing symptoms, such as fear or anxiety, worrying, and feeling self-conscious, while lower behavior loadings expressed increased externalizing symptoms, such as aggressivity and rule-breaking behaviors
source: Here, higher (i.e., positive) behavior loadings indicated increased internalizing symptoms, such as fear or anxiety, worrying, and feeling self-conscious, while lower (i.e., negative) behavior loadings expressed increased externalizing symptoms, such as aggressivity and rule-breaking behaviors (Figure 3b, Supplementary file 1b).

claim: Greater internalizing symptoms in LC2 were associated with widespread decreases in cortical thickness, and mixed patterns of increases and decreases in surface area and volume
source: At the brain level, greater internalizing symptoms were associated with widespread decreases in cortical thickness, and mixed patterns of increases and decreases in surface area and volume (Figure 3c).

claim: Worse internalizing symptoms in LC2 reflected lower RSFC within the somatomotor network and between the somatomotor and attention networks, and higher RSFC between the somatomotor network and the default and control networks
source: In terms of brain organization, worse internalizing symptoms reflected lower RSFC within the somatomotor network and between the somatomotor and attention networks, and higher RSFC between the somatomotor network and the default and control networks (Figure 3d).

claim: LC3 was driven by neurodevelopmental symptoms, such as concentration difficulties and inattention, daydreaming, and restlessness
source: LC3 (r = 0.35, permuted p < 0.001; out-of-sample generalizability of model statistics: r = 0.07, permuted p < 0.001; Figure 4a) was driven by neurodevelopmental symptoms, such as concentration difficulties and inattention, daydreaming, and restlessness (Figure 4b, Supplementary file 1b), which were contrasted to a mix of symptoms characterized by emotion dysregulation.

claim: Greater neurodevelopmental symptoms in LC3 were associated with increased surface area and volume in temporoparietal regions and decreased surface area and volume in prefrontal as well as in occipital regions
source: Greater neurodevelopmental symptoms were associated with increased surface area and volume in temporoparietal regions and decreased surface area and volume in prefrontal as well as in occipital regions, but also with increased thickness in temporo-occipital areas and decreased thickness in prefrontal regions (Figure 4c).

claim: Worse neurodevelopmental symptomatology in LC3 was related to decreased RSFC within most cortical networks such as the default, control, dorsal, and ventral attention, and somatomotor networks
source: Worse neurodevelopmental symptomatology was also related to decreased RSFC within most cortical networks such as the default, control, dorsal, and ventral attention, and somatomotor networks, and increased RSFC between control, default, and limbic networks on the one side, and attention and somatomotor networks on the other side (Figure 4d).

claim: The primary functional gradient explained 28% of the RSFC variance, and differentiated primary somatosensory/motor and visual areas from transmodal association cortices
source: The primary functional gradient explained 28% of the RSFC variance, and differentiated primary somatosensory/motor and visual areas from transmodal association cortices (Figure 5b).

claim: The primary functional gradient results replicated previous findings obtained with RSFC in a healthy adult cohort
source: These results replicated previous findings obtained with RSFC in a healthy adult cohort (Margulies et al., 2016).

claim: Between-network RSFC loadings for LC1 and LC3 showed a strong positive correlation to the principal gradient (LC1: r = 0.43, pspin < 0.001; LC3: r = 0.33, pspin < 0.001)
source: Between-network RSFC loadings for LC1 and LC3 showed a strong positive correlation to the principal gradient (LC1: r = 0.43, pspin < 0.001; LC3: r = 0.33, pspin < 0.001; Figure 5d), that is, between-network connectivity was higher in transmodal regions and lower in sensory areas.
evidence: Statistical correlation results with spin permutation testing

claim: Within-network RSFC loadings for LC1, LC2, and LC3 showed a significant albeit weak correlation with the sensory-to-transmodal gradient (LC1: r = −0.14, pspin = 0.010; LC2: r = 0.13, pspin = 0.032; LC3: r = 0.17, pspin = 0.017)
source: Within-network RSFC loadings for LC1, LC2, and LC3 also showed a significant albeit weak correlation with the sensory-to-transmodal gradient LC1: r = −0.14, pspin = 0.010; LC2: r = 0.13, pspin = 0.032; LC3: r = 0.17, pspin = 0.017 (Figure 5d), that is, within-network FC was higher in sensory regions in LC1, and in higher-order regions in LCs 2–3.
evidence: Statistical correlation results with spin permutation testing

claim: Greater psychopathology (LC1) was related to widespread decrease in FA and MD in all white matter tracts
source: Greater psychopathology (LC1) was related to widespread decrease in FA and MD in all white matter tracts (see Supplementary file 1e for diffusion-based loadings and Z-scores for all white matter tracts).

claim: Higher internalizing and lower externalizing symptoms (LC2) were associated to higher FA within the left superior corticostriate-frontal and corticostriate tracts, and higher MD within the foreceps major and parahippocampal cingulum
source: Higher internalizing and lower externalizing symptoms (LC2) were associated to higher FA within the left superior corticostriate-frontal and corticostriate tracts, and higher MD within the foreceps major and parahippocampal cingulum.

claim: Greater neurodevelopmental symptoms (LC3) were related to decreased FA within the right cingulate cingulum, and within the left superior, temporal, and parietal longitudinal fasciculus
source: Finally, greater neurodevelopmental symptoms (LC3) were related to decreased FA within the right cingulate cingulum, and within the left superior, temporal, and parietal longitudinal fasciculus.

claim: Greater psychopathology (LC1) was associated with higher FC between control and default network across all states, including rest
source: Greater psychopathology was associated with higher FC between control and default network across all states, including rest (Figure 6c).
evidence: Results from task-based functional connectivity analysis

claim: Male participants had higher imaging and behavior composite scores in LC1 (p factor) and LC3 (neurodevelopmental symptoms), while female participants had higher imaging and behavior composite scores in LC2 (internalizing symptoms)
source: Notably, we found that male participants had higher composite scores on LC1 (p factor) and LC3 (neurodevelopmental symptoms), while female participants had higher composite scores on LC2 (internalizing symptoms) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Both imaging and behavior scores for LC2 (internalizing/externalizing symptoms) were significantly albeit weakly correlated with age and age2 (r = 0.04–0.05, ps < 0.028)
source: Furthermore, both imaging and behavior scores for LC2 (internalizing/externalizing symptoms) were significantly albeit weakly correlated with age and age2 (r = 0.04–0.05, ps < 0.028; Supplementary file 1g).

claim: Significant correlations were observed between behavioral loadings of LCs 1–3 across discovery and replication samples (r = 0.63–0.97)
source: We observed significant correlations between behavioral loadings of LCs 1–3 across discovery and replication samples (r = 0.63–0.97).

claim: RSFC loadings were replicated in LCs 1–3 (r = 0.11–0.29, pspin < 0.05)
source: In terms of imaging loadings, RSFC loadings were replicated in LCs 1–3 (r = 0.11–0.29, pspin < 0.05)
evidence: Replication analysis results with spin permutation testing

claim: Thickness loadings were replicated in LCs 1–3 (r = 0.15–0.55, pspin < 0.05)
source: thickness loadings were replicated in LCs 1–3 (r = 0.15–0.55, pspin < 0.05)
evidence: Replication analysis results with spin permutation testing

claim: Volume loadings were replicated in LCs 1–2 (r = 0.18–0.19, pspin < 0.05) but not LC3 (r = 0.02, p = 0.467)
source: volume loadings were replicated in LCs 1–2 (r = 0.18–0.19, pspin < 0.05) but not LC3 (r = 0.02, p = 0.467)
evidence: Replication analysis results with spin permutation testing

claim: Surface area loadings were only replicated in LC2 (r = 0.15, pspin = 0.040)
source: finally, surface area loadings were only replicated in LC2 (r = 0.15, pspin = 0.040).
evidence: Replication analysis results with spin permutation testing

claim: Out-of-sample prediction was overall high across LCs 1–3 for behavioral loading (r = 0.94–0.97), and lower for imaging loadings (r = 0.16–0.29)
source: With this approach, we found that out-of-sample prediction was overall high across LCs 1–3 for behavioral loading (r = 0.94–0.97), and lower for imaging loadings (r = 0.16–0.29).

claim: Out-of-sample prediction statistics linking imaging features and behavior were generally low across LCs but remained statistically significant (LC1 r = 0.03; LC2 r = 0.05; LC3 r = 0.07; all permuted p < 0.001)
source: This lower replicability of brain features also affected out-of-sample prediction statistics linking imaging features and behavior (cross-validated composite scores), which were generally low across LCs but remained statistically significant (LC1 r = 0.03; LC2 r = 0.05; LC3 r = 0.07; all permuted p < 0.001 after permuting the first five LCs 10,000 times, accounting for site and FDR).
evidence: Out-of-sample prediction results with permutation testing

claim: The model exhibited relatively poor out-of-sample prediction performance
source: In this regard, our model was found to exhibit relatively poor out-of-sample prediction performance, as is often the case in explorations of complex brain–behavior relationships.

claim: Poor generalizability limits the potential of the present findings to meaningfully inform our understanding of the neural basis of psychopathology symptom dimensions and influence clinical practice
source: This poor generalizability limits the potential of the present findings to meaningfully inform our understanding of the neural basis of psychopathology symptom dimensions and influence clinical practice.
evidence: Interpretation of the implications of poor generalizability

claim: Late childhood is a period of major neurodevelopmental changes
source: Late childhood is a period of major neurodevelopmental changes (Goddings et al., 2014; Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011; Mills et al., 2021; Paus et al., 2008; Raznahan et al., 2011), which makes it particularly vulnerable for the emergence of mental illness.

claim: The Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) is a transdiagnostic framework to study the neurobiological underpinnings of dimensional constructs, by integrating findings from genetics, cognitive neuroscience, and neuroimaging
source: One key initiative is the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC), a transdiagnostic framework to study the neurobiological underpinnings of dimensional constructs, by integrating findings from genetics, cognitive neuroscience, and neuroimaging (Cuthbert, 2014; Insel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cuthbert, 2014; Insel et al., 2010

claim: A transdiagnostic approach in characterizing behavioral difficulties in children and adolescents might capture a broader subset of children at risk
source: From a neurodevelopmental perspective, a transdiagnostic approach in characterizing behavioral difficulties in children and adolescents might capture a broader subset of children at risk (Astle et al., 2022; Casey et al., 2014; Jones and Astle, 2021; Siugzdaite et al., 2020).

claim: A more quantitative approach to psychopathology could capture the entire range of variation (i.e., typical, subclinical, and atypical) in both symptom and brain data
source: Such a more quantitative approach to psychopathology could capture the entire range of variation (i.e., typical, subclinical, and atypical) in both symptom and brain data (Insel et al., 2010; Plomin et al., 2009), and help elucidate their ties (Parkes et al., 2020).

claim: The p factor reflects an individual's susceptibility to develop any common form of psychopathology
source: Psychopathology can be conceptualized along a hierarchical structure, with a general psychopathology (or p factor) at the apex, reflecting an individual's susceptibility to develop any common form of psychopathology (Caspi et al., 2014; Kotov et al., 2017; Lahey et al., 2017).

claim: Higher-order dimensions in the psychopathology hierarchy underpin internalizing behaviors, such as anxiety or depressive symptoms, as well as externalizing behaviors, characterized by rule-breaking and aggressive behavior
source: Next in this hierarchy are higher-order dimensions underpinning internalizing behaviors, such as anxiety or depressive symptoms, as well as externalizing behaviors, characterized by rule-breaking and aggressive behavior.
evidence: Description of psychopathology hierarchy based on established literature

claim: A neurodevelopmental dimension encompasses symptoms with shared genetic vulnerability, such as attention deficit/hyperactivity deficit (ADHD)-related symptoms, as well as clumsiness and autistic-like traits
source: Furthermore, a neurodevelopmental dimension has been described to encompass symptoms with shared genetic vulnerability, such as attention deficit/hyperactivity deficit (ADHD)-related symptoms (e.g., inattention and hyperactivity), as well as clumsiness and autistic-like traits.
evidence: Description of neurodevelopmental dimension based on literature

claim: The neurodevelopmental dimension might underpin the normal variation in ADHD- and autism spectrum disorder-like traits in the general population, but also learning disabilities
source: This dimension is particularly relevant as it might underpin the normal variation in ADHD- and autism spectrum disorder-like traits in the general population, but also learning disabilities (Holmes et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holmes et al., 2021

claim: The findings are largely consistent with the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP)
source: These findings are largely consistent with the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) (Kotov et al., 2017), a dimensional classification system that aims to provide more robust clinical targets than traditional taxonomies.
evidence: Comparison to established framework with citation

claim: Most neuroimaging studies have employed case–control comparisons between cohorts with a psychiatric diagnosis and neurotypical controls
source: To date, most neuroimaging studies have employed case–control comparisons between cohorts with a psychiatric diagnosis and neurotypical controls (Etkin, 2019).

claim: An increasing number of studies have adopted transdiagnostic neuroimaging designs in recent years
source: However, an increasing number of studies have adopted transdiagnostic neuroimaging designs in recent years (Baker et al., 2019; Elliott et al., 2018; Kebets et al., 2021; Kebets et al., 2019; Parkes et al., 2021; Romer and Pizzagalli, 2022; Xia et al., 2018).

claim: Combined assessments of structural and functional substrates of psychopathology remain scarce, specifically with a transdiagnostic design
source: Despite increasing availability of multimodal datasets (Casey et al., 2018; Jernigan et al., 2016; Miller et al., 2016; Royer et al., 2022; Satterthwaite et al., 2016; Thompson et al., 2014; Van Essen et al., 2013), combined assessments of structural and functional substrates of psychopathology remain scarce, specifically with a transdiagnostic design.
evidence: Observation about the literature with citations

claim: Unsupervised techniques such as partial least squares (PLS) or canonical correlation analysis may provide a data-driven integration of different imaging measures
source: In this context, unsupervised techniques such as partial least squares (PLS) or canonical correlation analysis, may provide a data-driven integration of different imaging measures, and allow for the identification of dimensional substrates of psychopathology along with potential neurobiological underpinnings.

claim: Recent work has pointed to a particular importance of the progressive differentiation between sensory/motor systems and transmodal association cortices, also referred to as sensory-to-transmodal or sensorimotor-to-association axis of cortical organization
source: Recent work integrating neuroanatomical, neurodevelopmental, and psychiatric data has furthermore pointed to a particular importance of the progressive differentiation between sensory/motor systems and transmodal association cortices, also referred to as sensory-to-transmodal or sensorimotor-to-association axis of cortical organization (Huntenburg et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016; Paquola et al., 2019; Park et al., 2022b; Sydnor et al., 2021).

claim: The maturation of association cortices underlies important changes in cognition, affect, and behavior, and has been suggested to highly contribute to inter-individual differences in functioning and risk for psychiatric disorders
source: Crucially, the maturation of association cortices underlies important changes in cognition, affect, and behavior, and has been suggested to highly contribute to inter-individual differences in functioning and risk for psychiatric disorders (Sydnor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sydnor et al., 2021

claim: Child psychopathology was characterized with the parent-reported Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL)
source: Child psychopathology was characterized with the parent-reported Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) (Achenbach and Rescorla, 2013).

claim: The study combined multiple intrinsic measures of brain structure (i.e., cortical surface area, thickness, and volume) and functional connectivity at rest in the primary analysis
source: To profile neural substrates, we combined multiple intrinsic measures of brain structure (i.e., cortical surface area, thickness, and volume) and functional connectivity at rest in our primary analysis.

claim: Post hoc analyses in smaller subsamples incorporated diffusion-based measures of fiber architecture (i.e., fractional anisotropy [FA] and mean diffusivity [MD]) and explored connectivity during tasks tapping into executive and reward processes
source: Post hoc analyses in smaller subsamples also incorporated diffusion-based measures of fiber architecture (i.e., fractional anisotropy [FA] and mean diffusivity [MD]) and explored connectivity during tasks tapping into executive and reward processes.

claim: The synergistic incorporation of multiple brain measures may capture multiple scales of brain organization during this critical developmental moment, and offer sensitivity in identifying neural signatures of psychopathology dimensions
source: We expected that the synergistic incorporation of multiple brain measures may capture multiple scales of brain organization during this critical developmental moment, and offer sensitivity in identifying neural signatures of psychopathology dimensions.

claim: The study examined if substrates of psychopathology followed the sensory-to-transmodal axis of cortical organization
source: We further examined if substrates of psychopathology followed the sensory-to-transmodal axis of cortical organization.

claim: The analysis was conducted in a Discovery subsample of the ABCD cohort, and validated in a Replication subsample from the same cohort
source: We conducted our analysis in a Discovery subsample of the ABCD cohort, and validated all findings in a Replication subsample from the same cohort.

claim: Applying model statistics derived from the Discovery cohort to unseen data of the Replication cohort revealed low generalizability and explained variance in brain–behavior relationships
source: Applying model statistics derived from the Discovery cohort to unseen data of the Replication cohort revealed, however, low generalizability and explained variance in brain–behavior relationships.

claim: Structural and functional measures of brain organization represent biologically meaningful phenotypes capturing distinct evolutionary, genetic, and cellular processes
source: Our study combined multiple measures tapping on brain structure that represent biologically meaningful phenotypes capturing distinct evolutionary, genetic, and cellular processes (Raznahan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raznahan et al., 2011

claim: Structural brain processes follow a nonlinear (i.e., a curvilinear inverted-U) trajectory during neurodevelopment that peak in late childhood/adolescence
source: These processes are closely intertwined, and follow a nonlinear (i.e., a curvilinear inverted-U) trajectory during neurodevelopment that peak in late childhood/adolescence (Raznahan et al., 2011) – but how and when these processes are disturbed by psychopathology is still poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to Raznahan et al., 2011

claim: The integrated approach replicated the dimensions found by Michelini et al., 2019, thereby extending them to a wide range of neurobiological substrates
source: Our integrated approach nevertheless replicated the dimensions found by Michelini et al., 2019, thereby extending them to a wide range of neurobiological substrates.
evidence: Comparison to prior work with citation

claim: The findings recapitulated the hierarchy within psychopathology, with the p factor explaining the highest covariance across multiple imaging features
source: Moreover, our findings recapitulated the hierarchy within psychopathology (Kotov et al., 2017; Lahey et al., 2017), with the p factor explaining the highest covariance across multiple imaging features, and distinct structural and functional signatures related to internalizing, externalizing, and neurodevelopmental dimensions.

claim: Previous research had found that disentangling the variation due to the p factor from other dimensions could be challenging, with sometimes few morphological or connectivity changes related to second-order dimensions left after adjusting for the p factor
source: Previous research had found that disentangling the variation due to the p factor from other dimensions could be challenging, with sometimes few morphological or connectivity changes related to second-order dimensions left after adjusting for the p factor (e.g., Cui et al., 2021; Parkes et al., 2021).

claim: By using PLS, which derives orthogonal components, the study ensured that the neural substrates associated with LCs 2–5 were independent from those associated with the p factor (i.e., LC1)
source: By using PLS, which derives orthogonal components (McIntosh and Lobaugh, 2004; McIntosh and Mišić, 2013), we ensured that the neural substrates associated with LCs 2–5 were independent from those associated with the p factor (i.e., LC1).

claim: Structural patterns associated with psychopathology dimensions were highly similar across structural modalities, and somewhat similar to functional patterns though to a much lesser extent
source: Furthermore, we observed that structural patterns associated with psychopathology dimensions were highly similar across structural modalities, and somewhat similar to functional patterns though to a much lesser extent, which further suggests that structural and functional modalities provide complementary information to characterize vulnerability to psychopathology.

claim: The p factor was associated with widespread decreases in cortical thickness, volume, but also in FA and MD
source: The p factor was associated with widespread decreases in cortical thickness, volume, but also in FA and MD.

claim: The pattern of widespread decreases in cortical thickness, volume, FA and MD likely reflects a general effect of atypical brain morphology associated with worse overall functioning
source: In line with previous research, this pattern likely reflects a general effect of atypical brain morphology associated with worse overall functioning (Kaczkurkin et al., 2019; Romer et al., 2021).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to prior work

claim: Increased FC between control and default networks was found across all cognitive states – a pattern of dysconnectivity that had previously been reported across dimensions of mood, psychosis, fear, and externalizing behavior
source: At the functional level, increased FC between control and default networks was found across all cognitive states – a pattern of dysconnectivity that had previously been reported across dimensions of mood, psychosis, fear, and externalizing behavior (Xia et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison to prior work with citation

claim: Cortical thickness patterns for LC2 were consistent with a recent study reporting increased frontotemporal thickness associated with externalizing behavior in the same cohort
source: Cortical thickness patterns were consistent with a recent study reporting increased frontotemporal thickness associated with externalizing behavior in the same cohort (Modabbernia et al., 2022).
evidence: Comparison to prior work with citation

claim: The three broad dimensions (i.e., p factor, internalizing, externalizing) are thought to be underpinned by sets of pleiotropic genetic influences that characterize the principal modes of genetic risk transmission for most disorders in childhood and adolescence
source: These three broad dimensions (i.e., p factor, internalizing, externalizing) are thought to be underpinned by sets of pleiotropic genetic influences that characterize the principal modes of genetic risk transmission for most disorders in childhood and adolescence (Pettersson et al., 2016; Pettersson et al., 2013), as well as by environmental events and contextual factors, such as familial situation, trauma, and broader socioeconomic challenges, which may collectively modulate the way these disorders are expressed (Gur et al., 2019).

claim: The neurodevelopmental component has previously been linked to intelligence and academic achievement
source: The third component resembled the neurodevelopmental dimension, which captures inattention and autistic traits, and has previously been linked to intelligence and academic achievement (Kim et al., 2018; Michelini et al., 2021; Michelini et al., 2019), and more generally a predictor of learning (Holmes et al., 2021).

claim: The neurodevelopmental component was characterized by decreased within-network RSFC patterns across all cognitive states, in line with previous finding in the same cohort reporting lower RSFC within the default mode network, and altered connectivity of the default and control networks in association with neurodevelopmental symptoms
source: At the functional level, the neurodevelopmental component was characterized by decreased within-network RSFC patterns across all cognitive states, in line with previous finding in the same cohort reporting lower RSFC within the default mode network, and altered connectivity of the default and control networks in association with neurodevelopmental symptoms (Karcher et al., 2021).
evidence: Comparison to prior work with citation

claim: The findings add evidence to neurodevelopmental symptoms having common neurobiological substrates that are distinct from other psychiatric disorders
source: Our findings add evidence to this cluster of symptoms having common neurobiological substrates that are distinct from other psychiatric disorders (Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2019; Opel et al., 2020), which is in line with the known broad genetic overlap between neurodevelopmental symptoms, including autistic and ADHD behaviors, as well as learning difficulties, both throughout the general population and at the quantitative extreme (Pettersson et al., 2013; Ronald et al., 2008).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to prior work

claim: There is significant phenotypic overlap in the general population between autistic traits and ADHD symptoms
source: There is also significant phenotypic overlap in the general population between autistic traits and ADHD symptoms, a co-occurrence that might be due to the disruptions in brain development during critical stages in gestation, infancy or early childhood, which could in turn lead to problems that would affect the normal growth process in areas such as learning, social interaction and behavioral control – a process that is primarily genetic in origin (Ronald et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ronald et al., 2008

claim: A recent study found that polygenic risk scores for ADHD and autism were associated with the neurodevelopmental factor in the ABCD cohort, although the latter did not survive after adjusting for the p factor
source: A recent study found that polygenic risk scores for ADHD and autism were associated with the neurodevelopmental factor in the ABCD cohort, although the latter did not survive after adjusting for the p factor (Waszczuk et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waszczuk et al., 2023

claim: One major dimension of cortical organization situates large-scale networks along a spectrum running from unimodal regions supporting action and perception to heteromodal association areas implicated in abstract cognition
source: One major dimension situates large-scale networks along a spectrum running from unimodal regions supporting action and perception to heteromodal association areas implicated in abstract cognition (Margulies et al., 2016; Paquola et al., 2019).

claim: The sensory-to-transmodal gradient was initially demonstrated at the level of intrinsic functional connectivity
source: Initially demonstrated at the level of intrinsic functional connectivity (Margulies et al., 2016), follow-up work confirmed a similar cortical patterning using microarchitectural in vivo MRI indices related to cortical myelination (Burt et al., 2018; Huntenburg et al., 2017; Paquola et al., 2019), post-mortem cytoarchitecture (Goulas et al., 2018; Paquola et al., 2020; Paquola et al., 2019), or post-mortem microarray gene expression (Burt et al., 2018).

claim: Spatiotemporal patterns in the formation and maturation of large-scale networks have been found to follow a similar sensory-to-association axis
source: Spatiotemporal patterns in the formation and maturation of large-scale networks have been found to follow a similar sensory-to-association axis; moreover, there is the emerging view that this framework may offer key insights into brain plasticity and susceptibility to psychopathology (Sydnor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sydnor et al., 2021

claim: The increased vulnerability of transmodal association cortices in late childhood and early adolescence has been suggested to relate to prolonged maturation and potential for plastic reconfigurations of these systems
source: In particular, the increased vulnerability of transmodal association cortices in late childhood and early adolescence has been suggested to relate to prolonged maturation and potential for plastic reconfigurations of these systems (Paquola et al., 2019; Park et al., 2022b).

claim: Between mid-childhood and early adolescence, heteromodal association systems such as the default network become progressively more integrated among distant regions, while being more differentiated from spatially adjacent systems
source: Between mid-childhood and early adolescence, heteromodal association systems such as the default network become progressively more integrated among distant regions, while being more differentiated from spatially adjacent systems, paralleling the development of cognitive control, as well as increasingly abstract and logical thinking.
evidence: Statement about developmental neuroscience based on established knowledge

claim: The fine-tuning of heteromodal association systems is underpinned by a gradual differentiation between higher- and lower-order regions, which may be dependent on the maturation of association cortices
source: This fine-tuning is underpinned by a gradual differentiation between higher- and lower-order regions, which may be dependent on the maturation of association cortices.

claim: The maturational variability of association cortices is thought to underpin inter-individual variability in psychosocial functioning and mental illness
source: As they subserve cognitive, mentalizing, and socioemotional processes, their maturational variability is thought to underpin inter-individual variability in psychosocial functioning and mental illness (Sydnor et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sydnor et al., 2021

claim: Between-network RSFC loadings related to the p factor followed the sensory-to-transmodal gradient, with the default and control networks yielding higher between-network FC (i.e., greater integration) while sensory systems exhibited lower between-network FC (i.e., greater segregation)
source: We found that between-network RSFC loadings related to the p factor followed the sensory-to-transmodal gradient, with the default and control networks yielding higher between-network FC (i.e., greater integration) while sensory systems exhibited lower between-network FC (i.e., greater segregation), suggesting that connectivity between the two anchors of the principal gradient might be affected by the p factor.

claim: The finding that between-network RSFC loadings related to the p factor followed the sensory-to-transmodal gradient is in line with recent studies showing that the sensory-to-transmodal axis is impacted across several disorders
source: This finding is in line with recent studies showing that the sensory-to-transmodal axis is impacted across several disorders (Hettwer et al., 2022; Opel et al., 2020; Park et al., 2022a).
evidence: Comparison to prior work with citations

claim: The p factor represents a general liability to all common forms of psychopathology
source: As the p factor represents a general liability to all common forms of psychopathology, this points toward a disorder-general biomarker of dysconnectivity between lower- and higher-order systems in the cortical hierarchy (Elliott et al., 2018; Kebets et al., 2019), which might be due to abnormal differentiation between higher- and lower-order brain networks, possibly reflective of atypical maturation of higher-order networks.

claim: A similar pattern of association with the sensory-to-transmodal gradient, albeit somewhat weaker, was also observed in association with the neurodevelopmental dimension
source: Interestingly, a similar pattern, albeit somewhat weaker, was also observed in association with the neurodevelopmental dimension.

claim: Neurodevelopmental difficulties might be related to alterations in various processes orchestrated by sensory and association regions, as well as the macroscale balance and hierarchy of these systems
source: This suggests that neurodevelopmental difficulties might be related to alterations in various processes orchestrated by sensory and association regions, as well as the macroscale balance and hierarchy of these systems, in line with previous findings in several neurodevelopmental conditions, including autism, schizophrenia, as well as epilepsy, showing a decreased differentiation between the two anchors of this gradient (Hong et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretation with citation to prior work

claim: The compact and low-dimensional perspective of gradients may provide beneficial in terms of biomarker reliability as well as phenotypic prediction
source: In particular, the compact and low-dimensional perspective of gradients may provide beneficial in terms of biomarker reliability as well as phenotypic prediction, as previously demonstrated using typically developing cohorts (Hong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2020

claim: Alterations in connectivity along sensory-to-transmodal hierarchies mainly reflect risk for general psychopathology and atypical development
source: On the other hand, it will be of interest to explore in how far alterations in connectivity along sensory-to-transmodal hierarchies provide sufficient granularity to differentiate between specific psychopathologies, or whether they, as the current work suggests, mainly reflect risk for general psychopathology and atypical development.

claim: Latent variable approaches such as PLS do not inform on any causal associations between datasets
source: First, latent variable approaches such as PLS are powerful methods to characterize modes of covariation between multiple datasets, but they do not inform on any causal associations between them.

claim: Verifying findings in an independent dataset other than ABCD would indicate broader generalizability
source: Second, although they were repeated in a replication cohort, verifying our findings in an independent dataset other than ABCD would indicate broader generalizability.

claim: The study only considered the ABCD cohort's baseline data
source: Furthermore, we only considered the ABCD cohort's baseline data in our analyses; longitudinal models assessing multiple time points will enable to further model developmental trajectories, test the stability of these dimensions over time, and how they relate to clinical phenotypes (Brieant et al., 2022; Leban, 2021).
evidence: Statement about study limitations with citations

claim: Brain–environment interactions likely reinforce one another throughout development in shaping different forms of psychopathology
source: Our approach could be expanded to consider brain–environment interactions, as they likely reinforce one another throughout development in shaping different forms of psychopathology (Sprooten et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sprooten et al., 2022

claim: A recent study in the same cohort has shown that a broad range of environmental risk factors, including perinatal complications, socio-demographics, urbanization, and pollution, characterized the main modes of variation in brain imaging phenotypes
source: For instance, a recent study in the same cohort has shown that a broad range of environmental risk factors, including perinatal complications, socio-demographics, urbanization, and pollution, characterized the main modes of variation in brain imaging phenotypes (Alnæs et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alnæs et al., 2020

claim: Other factors have been suggested to impact the development of psychopathology, such as executive functioning deficits, earlier pubertal timing, negative life events, maternal depression, or psychological factors
source: Other factors have also been suggested to impact the development of psychopathology, such as executive functioning deficits (Zelazo, 2020), earlier pubertal timing (Ullsperger and Nikolas, 2017), negative life events (Brieant et al., 2021), maternal depression (Goodman and Gotlib, 1999; Goodman et al., 2011), or psychological factors (e.g., low effortful control, high neuroticism, and negative affectivity) (Lynch et al., 2021).

claim: Biases of caregiver reports have been shown with potential divergences between the child's and parent's report depending on family conflict
source: Moreover, biases of caregiver reports have been shown with potential divergences between the child's and parent's report depending on family conflict (Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen et al., 2021

claim: A large number of missing data in the teachers' reports prevented validation of brain–behavior associations with a second caretaker's report
source: A large number of missing data in the teachers' reports prevented us from validating these brain–behavior associations with a second caretaker's report.

claim: Prior research has shown that resting-state fMRI networks may be affected by differences in instructions and study paradigm
source: Finally, while prior research has shown that resting-state fMRI networks may be affected by differences in instructions and study paradigm (e.g., with respect to eyes open vs. closed) (Agcaoglu et al., 2019), the resting-state fMRI paradigm is homogenized in the ABCD study to be passive viewing of a centrally presented fixation cross.
evidence: Supported by citation to Agcaoglu et al., 2019

claim: There is a mounting literature based on high-definition fMRI acquisitions suggesting that functional networks are mainly dominated by common organizational principles and stable individual features, with substantially more modest contributions from task-state variability
source: Notably, however, there is a mounting literature based on high-definition fMRI acquisitions suggesting that functional networks are mainly dominated by common organizational principles and stable individual features, with substantially more modest contributions from task-state variability (Gratton et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gratton et al., 2020

claim: Resting-state fMRI markers can serve as powerful phenotypes of psychiatric conditions, and potential biomarkers
source: These findings, thus, suggest that resting-state fMRI markers can serve as powerful phenotypes of psychiatric conditions, and potential biomarkers (Abraham et al., 2017; Gratton et al., 2020; Parkes et al., 2020).

claim: The study identified several dimensions of psychopathology which recapitulated the psychopathological hierarchy, alongside their structural and functional neural substrates
source: Despite these limitations, our study identified several dimensions of psychopathology which recapitulated the psychopathological hierarchy, alongside their structural and functional neural substrates.

claim: The findings are a first step toward capturing multimodal neurobiological changes underpinning broad dimensions of psychopathology, which might be used to predict future psychiatric diagnosis
source: These findings are a first step toward capturing multimodal neurobiological changes underpinning broad dimensions of psychopathology, which might be used to predict future psychiatric diagnosis.

claim: Data were collected from 11,875 children from the ABCD 2.0.1 release
source: We considered data from 11,875 children from the ABCD 2.0.1 release.

claim: The ABCD data were collected on 21 sites across the United States
source: The data were collected on 21 sites across the United States (https://abcdstudy.org/contact/), and aimed to be representative of the socio-demographic diversity of the US population of 9–10 year old children (Garavan et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about data collection with citation

claim: Ethical review and approval of the ABCD protocol was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at the University of California, San Diego, as well as from local IRB
source: Ethical review and approval of the protocol was obtained from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at the University of California, San Diego, as well as from local IRB (Auchter et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about ethical approval with citation

claim: Parents/guardians and children provided written assent for the ABCD study
source: Parents/guardians and children provided written assent (Clark et al., 2018).

claim: The parent-reported CBCL is comprised of 119 items that measure various symptoms in the child's behavior in the past 6 months
source: The parent-reported CBCL (Achenbach and Rescorla, 2013) is comprised of 119 items that measure various symptoms in the child's behavior in the past 6 months.
evidence: Description of assessment tool with citation

claim: CBCL symptoms are rated on a three-point scale from (0 = not true, 1 = somewhat or sometimes true, 2 = very true or always true)
source: Symptoms are rated on a three-point scale from (0 = not true, 1 = somewhat or sometimes true, 2 = very true or always true).

claim: The study used 118/119 CBCL items; one item was removed ('Smokes, chews, or sniffs tobacco') as all participants from the discovery sample scored '0' for this question
source: We used 118/119 items (see Supplementary file 1h for a complete list of items); one item was removed ('Smokes, chews, or sniffs tobacco') as all participants from the discovery sample scored '0' for this question.

claim: Effects of age, age2, sex, site, and ethnicity were regressed out from the behavioral and imaging data using a multiple linear regression
source: Prior to the PLS analysis, effects of age, age2, sex, site, and ethnicity were regressed out from the behavioral and imaging data using a multiple linear regression to ensure that the LCs would not be driven by possible socio-demographic confounders (Kebets et al., 2021; Kebets et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2018).

claim: The inclusion of ethnicity as a covariate in imaging studies has been recently called into question
source: Of note, the inclusion of ethnicity as a covariate in imaging studies has been recently called into question (Saragosa-Harris et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saragosa-Harris et al., 2022

claim: Ethnicity was included in the main model as a proxy for social inequalities relating to race and ethnicity alongside biological factors (age and sex) with documented effects on brain organization and neurodevelopmental symptomatology
source: In the present study, we included this variable in our main model as a proxy for social inequalities relating to race and ethnicity alongside biological factors (age and sex) with documented effects on brain organization and neurodevelopmental symptomatology queried in the CBCL.

claim: MR images were acquired across 21 sites in the United States with harmonized imaging protocols for GE, Philips, and Siemens scanners
source: MR images were acquired across 21 sites in the United States with harmonized imaging protocols for GE, Philips, and Siemens scanners (Casey et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of data acquisition with citation

claim: Scans acquired on the Philips scanner were excluded due to incorrect processing, as recommended by the ABCD consortium
source: Scans acquired on the Philips scanner were excluded due to incorrect processing, as recommended by the ABCD consortium.

claim: Real-time motion detection and correction were implemented for the structural scans and for rs-fMRI at the Siemens sites
source: As head motion is an important concern for (pediatric) imaging, real-time motion detection and correction were implemented for the structural scans and for rs-fMRI at the Siemens sites.

claim: Twenty minutes of rs-fMRI data were acquired in four runs, and participants were instructed to keep their eyes open while passively watching a cross hair on the screen
source: Twenty minutes of rs-fMRI data were acquired in four runs, and participants were instructed to keep their eyes open while passively watching a cross hair on the screen.

claim: The three fMRI tasks included an MID task, which measures domains of reward processing, an EN-back task which engages memory and emotion processing, and an SST that engages impulsivity and impulse control
source: The three fMRI tasks included an MID task, which measures domains of reward processing, an EN-back task which engages memory and emotion processing, and an SST that engages impulsivity and impulse control.

claim: Diffusion MR images included 96 diffusion directions, seven b = 0 frames, and four b-values
source: Diffusion MR images were acquired using a multiband EPI sequence (slice acceleration factor 3) and included 96 diffusion directions, seven b = 0 frames, and four b-values (6 directions with b = 500 s/mm2, 15 directions with b = 1000 s/mm2, 15 directions with b = 2000 s/mm2, and 60 directions with b = 3000 s/mm2).

claim: The study used minimally preprocessed T1w, fMRI, and diffusion MRI data
source: We used minimally preprocessed T1w, fMRI, and diffusion MRI data (Hagler et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of data preprocessing with citation

claim: T1w images underwent gradient warp correction, bias field correction, and were resampled to a reference brain in standard space with isotropic voxels
source: T1w images underwent gradient warp correction, bias field correction, and were resampled to a reference brain in standard space with isotropic voxels (Hagler et al., 2019).
evidence: Description of preprocessing steps with citation

claim: T1w images were further processed using FreeSurfer 5.3.0
source: They were further processed using FreeSurfer 5.3.0 (Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 1999a; Fischl et al., 1999b; Ségonne et al., 2004; Ségonne et al., 2007).
evidence: Description of preprocessing software with citations

claim: Cortical surface meshes were generated for each participant, and registered to a common spherical coordinate system
source: Cortical surface meshes were generated for each participant, and registered to a common spherical coordinate system (Fischl et al., 1999a, Fischl et al., 1999b).
evidence: Description of preprocessing steps with citations

claim: Participants that did not pass recon-all quality control were excluded
source: Participants that did not pass recon-all quality control were excluded.

claim: Runs with boundary-based registration cost >0.6 were excluded
source: Runs with boundary-based registration cost >0.6 were excluded.

claim: Frames with FD >0.3 mm or DVARS >50, along with one frame before and two frames after, were considered as outliers and subsequently censored
source: Frames with FD >0.3 mm or DVARS >50, along with one frame before and two frames after, were considered as outliers and subsequently censored.

claim: Runs with >50% frames censored and/or max FD >5 mm were excluded
source: Runs with >50% frames censored and/or max FD >5 mm were excluded.

claim: Participants with less than 4 min of fMRI data were removed
source: Participants with less than 4 min of data were also removed.

claim: Nuisance covariates including global signal, six motion parameters, averaged ventricular and white matter signal, along with their temporal derivates, were regressed out of the fMRI time series
source: Nuisance covariates including global signal, six motion parameters, averaged ventricular and white matter signal, along with their temporal derivates, were regressed out of the fMRI time series.

claim: Data were interpolated across censored frames using least squares spectral estimation
source: Data were interpolated across censored frames using least squares spectral estimation (Power et al., 2014).
evidence: Description of preprocessing steps with citation

claim: A bandpass filter (0.009–0.08 Hz) was applied to fMRI data
source: A bandpass filter (0.009–0.08 Hz) was applied.

claim: Preprocessed fMRI time series were projected onto FreeSurfer fsaverage6 surface space and smoothed using a 6-mm full-width half maximum kernel
source: Finally, preprocessed time series were projected onto FreeSurfer fsaverage6 surface space and smoothed using a 6-mm full-width half maximum kernel.

claim: Major white matter tracts were labeled using AtlasTrack, a probabilistic atlas-based method for automated segmentation
source: Major white matter tracts were labeled using AtlasTrack, a probabilistic atlas-based method for automated segmentation (Hagler et al., 2009).
evidence: Description of processing method with citation

claim: Processed diffusion MRI data were available in 10,186 participants, among which 3275 overlapped with the Discovery sample (93%)
source: Processed diffusion MRI data were available in 10,186 participants, among which 3275 overlapped with the Discovery sample (93%).

claim: RSFC was computed as the Pearson's correlation between the average timeseries among 400 cortical and 19 subcortical regions, yielding 87,571 connections for each participant
source: RSFC was computed as the Pearson's correlation between the average timeseries among 400 cortical (Schaefer et al., 2018) and 19 subcortical (Fischl et al., 2002) regions (Figure 1a), yielding 87,571 connections for each participant.
evidence: Description of analysis method with citations

claim: Surface area, thickness, and volume were extracted from 400 cortical regions
source: Surface area, thickness, and volume were extracted from the same 400 cortical regions (Schaefer et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of feature extraction with citation

claim: Cortical thickness and volume measures were additionally adjusted for total intracranial volume, and surface area additionally for total surface area
source: Age, age2, sex, site, and ethnicity were also regressed out from each parcel-wise structural measure; cortical thickness and volume measures were additionally adjusted for total intracranial volume, and surface area additionally for total surface area.

claim: PCA was applied over each imaging feature, and PCA scores of the number of components explaining 50% of the variance within each data modality were selected before concatenating them
source: To reduce data dimensionality before combining the different imaging modalities, we applied PCA over each feature (i.e., surface area, cortical thickness, cortical volume, and RSFC), and selected PCA scores of the number of components explaining 50% of the variance within each data modality, before concatenating them (see Figure 1b).

claim: The dimensionality reduction yielded 50, 58, 57, and 256 principal components for surface area, thickness, volume, and RSFC, respectively, resulting in 421 components in total
source: We obtained 50, 58, 57, and 256 principal components for surface area, thickness, volume, and RSFC, respectively, resulting in 421 components in total.

claim: PLS correlation analysis was used to identify latent components (LCs) that optimally related children's symptoms to structural and functional imaging features
source: PLS correlation analysis (McIntosh and Lobaugh, 2004; McIntosh and Mišić, 2013) was used to identify latent components (LCs) that optimally related children's symptoms (indexed by the CBCL) to structural and functional imaging features (Figure 1c).
evidence: Description of analysis method with citations

claim: PLS is a multivariate data-driven statistical technique that aims to maximize the covariance between two data matrices by linearly projecting the behavioral and imaging data into a low-dimensional space
source: PLS is a multivariate data-driven statistical technique that aims to maximize the covariance between two data matrices by linearly projecting the behavioral and imaging data into a low-dimensional space.

claim: Statistical significance of the LCs was assessed using permutation testing (10,000 permutations accounting for site) over the singular values of the first five LCs
source: Statistical significance of the LCs was assessed using permutation testing (10,000 permutations accounting for site) over the singular values of the first five LCs, while accounting for acquisition site (i.e., data were permuted between participants from the same site).

claim: Loading stability was determined using bootstraps, whereby data were sampled 1000 times with replacement among participants from the same site
source: Loading stability was determined using bootstraps, whereby data were sampled 1000 times with replacement among participants from the same site.

claim: Bootstrapped Z-scores were computed by dividing each loading by its bootstrapped standard deviation
source: Bootstrapped Z-scores were computed by dividing each loading by its bootstrapped standard deviation.

claim: The bootstrapped Z-scores were converted to p-values and FDR-corrected (q < 0.05) along with other posthoc tests
source: The bootstrapped Z-scores were converted to p-values and FDR-corrected (q < 0.05) along with other posthoc tests.

claim: Diffusion map embedding was applied to the RSFC data to map psychopathology-related structural and functional abnormalities along the sensory-to-transmodal gradient of brain organization
source: To map psychopathology-related structural and functional abnormalities along the sensory-to-transmodal gradient of brain organization, we applied diffusion map embedding (Coifman et al., 2005), a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique to the RSFC data.
evidence: Description of analysis method with citation

claim: Spatial gradients of RSFC variations derived from nonlinear dimensionality reduction recapitulate the putative cortical hierarchy
source: Previous work has shown that spatial gradients of RSFC variations derived from nonlinear dimensionality reduction recapitulate the putative cortical hierarchy (Bernhardt et al., 2022; Margulies et al., 2016; Mesulam, 1998), suggesting that functional gradients might approximate an inherent coordinate system of the human cortex.

claim: A cosine similarity matrix was calculated from the average RSFC matrix of the full sample (i.e., discovery and replication samples together, N = 5,251)
source: To derive the functional gradient, we first calculated a cosine similarity matrix from the average RSFC matrix of our full sample (i.e., discovery and replication samples together, N = 5,251).

claim: The RSFC was initially thresholded to only contain the top 10% entries for each row, that is, the 10% strongest connections of each region
source: Following prior studies (Margulies et al., 2016), the RSFC was initially thresholded to only contain the top 10% entries for each row, that is, the 10% strongest connections of each region.
evidence: Description of analysis procedure with citation

claim: The connectivity gradient derived from the ABCD sample was aligned to gradients derived from the HCP healthy young adult dataset using Procrustes alignment
source: To facilitate comparison with previous work (Margulies et al., 2016), the connectivity gradient we derived from our ABCD sample was aligned to gradients derived from the HCP healthy young adult dataset, available in the BrainSpace toolbox (de Wael et al., 2020), using Procrustes alignment.
evidence: Description of analysis procedure with citations

claim: Pearson's correlations were computed between cortical PLS loadings (within each imaging modality) and scores from the first gradient
source: Finally, for gradient-based contextualization of our findings, we computed Pearson's correlations between cortical PLS loadings (within each imaging modality) and scores from the first gradient (i.e., recapitulating the sensory-to-transmodal axis of cortical organization).

claim: Statistical significance of spatial associations was assessed using 1000 spin tests that control for spatial autocorrelations, followed by FDR correction for multiple comparisons (q < 0.05)
source: Statistical significance of spatial associations was assessed using 1000 spin tests that control for spatial autocorrelations (Alexander-Bloch et al., 2018), followed by FDR correction for multiple comparisons (q < 0.05).
evidence: Description of statistical testing procedure with citation

claim: Task FC was computed across the entire timecourse of each fMRI task (thereby capturing both the active task and rest conditions)
source: Following the same pipeline as for the rs-fMRI data, FC was computed across the entire timecourse of each fMRI task (thereby capturing both the active task and rest conditions), that is, the MID task, which measures domains of reward processing, the EN-back task, which evaluates memory and emotion processing, and the SST, which engages impulsivity and impulse control.

claim: After excluding subjects that did not pass both rs- and task-fMRI quality control, MID and SST data were available in 2039 participants, while EN-back data were available in 3435 participants
source: After excluding subjects that did not pass both rs- and task-fMRI quality control, MID and SST data were available in 2039 participants, while EN-back data were available in 3435 participants.

claim: A total of 1195 of participants overlapped across the three tasks and the discovery sample (39%)
source: A total of 1195 of participants overlapped across the three tasks and the discovery sample (39%).

claim: Diffusion tensor metrics included FA and MD in 35 white matter tracts
source: Diffusion tensor metrics included FA and MD in 35 white matter tracts (Hagler et al., 2009).
evidence: Description of imaging metrics with citation

claim: FA measures directionally constrained diffusion of water molecules within the white matter and MD the overall diffusivity, and both metrics have been suggested to index fiber architecture and microstructure
source: FA measures directionally constrained diffusion of water molecules within the white matter and MD the overall diffusivity, and both metrics have been suggested to index fiber architecture and microstructure.
evidence: Description of imaging metrics based on established knowledge

claim: The contribution of task FC and diffusion MRI features was computed by correlating participants' task FC and diffusion MRI data with their imaging and behavior composite scores (from the main PLS analysis using structural and RSFC features)
source: The contribution of task FC and diffusion MRI features was computed by correlating participants' task FC and diffusion MRI data with their imaging and behavior composite scores (from the main PLS analysis using structural and RSFC features).

claim: The PLS analysis was repeated in the replication sample (N = 1,747, i.e., 1/3 of the sample), and the reliability of findings was tested by computing Pearson's correlations between the obtained behavior/imaging loadings with the original loadings
source: First, we repeated the PLS analysis in the replication sample (N = 1,747, i.e., 1/3 of our sample), and tested the reliability of our findings by computing Pearson's correlations between the obtained behavior/imaging loadings with the original loadings.

claim: The generalizability of findings was assessed by applying model weights computed in the discovery sample to the replication sample data
source: We also assessed the generalizability of our findings by applying model weights computed in the discovery sample to the replication sample data.

claim: The main PLS analysis was repeated while excluding cortical volume from imaging metrics to account for redundancy within structural imaging metrics
source: Third, to account for redundancy within structural imaging metrics included in our main PLS model (i.e., cortical volume is a result of both thickness and surface area), we also repeated our main analysis while excluding cortical volume from our imaging metrics.

claim: Manual quality control ratings were considered as a measure of T1w scan quality and included as a covariate in a multiple linear regression model
source: We also considered manual quality control ratings as a measure of T1w scan quality. This metric was included as a covariate in a multiple linear regression model accounting for potential confounds in the structural imaging data, in addition to age, age2, sex, site, ethnicity, intracranial volume (ICV), and total surface area.

claim: Effects of age and sex differences on the LCs were assessed by computing associations between participants' imaging/behavior composite scores and their age and sex, using either t-tests (for associations with sex) or Pearson's correlations (for associations with age)
source: We also further assessed the effects of socio-demographic profiles of our participant sample. Effects of age and sex differences on the LCs were assessed by computing associations between participants' imaging/behavior composite scores and their age and sex, using either t-tests (for associations with sex) or Pearson's correlations (for associations with age).

claim: The replicability of findings was assessed when removing race and ethnicity covariates prior to computing the PLS analysis and correlating imaging and behavioral composite scores across both models
source: We also assessed the replicability of our findings when removing race and ethnicity covariates prior to computing the PLS analysis and correlating imaging and behavioral composite scores across both models.
